sentences.text: Revenue, net interest income plus noninterest income, grew from $21.0 billion in FY2016 to $28.5 billion in FY2025, a 3.5% CAGR [D5][D219].
The path was not smooth: revenue was flat at $22.7 billion in FY2021, then jumped 15.8% in FY2023 to $28.0 billion [D117][D169][D189].
The FY2023 step change came from higher rates on earning assets and the MUB acquisition, which lifted net interest income 18.1% [D184][P33].
FY2024 reversed 2.4% as higher rates on deposit mix and pricing cut net interest income 6.4% [D214][D209][P21].
FY2025 recovered 4.4% on loan growth, fixed asset repricing and lower deposit rates [D239][P16].
Payment Services was the steadiest engine, growing 5.4% in FY2025 to $7.4 billion, 25.8% of revenue and +1.4pp of growth [S61][D259][D260][D261].
That segment's net revenue rose on higher average loan balances and lower funding costs, plus merchant processing and card revenue from higher sales volume [P4].
Consumer and Business Banking shrank 3.9% in FY2025, subtracting 1.3pp, as deposit mix and second-quarter loan sales cut net interest income [D252][D253][P6].
Noninterest income outgrew net interest income in FY2025, 7.6% against 2.2%, lifting its share of revenue [D235][D234].
Net income grew 20.2% against 4.4% revenue growth, so costs fell faster than revenue [D227][D239].
The efficiency ratio was 59.0% in FY2025, just below its 59.3% window median and far under the 67.4% FY2023 high [D220][D277][D276].
It ranks at the 14th percentile of seven banks peers, better than the 61.7% peer median [D280][D281].
Noninterest expense fell 2.0% in FY2025 on prior-year merger and FDIC charges and lower compensation, partly offset by technology and marketing spend [D238][P10].
The FY2023 efficiency spike to 67.4% came from merger and integration charges, the $734 million FDIC special assessment and MUB operating costs [D170][P30].
The FY2025 tax rate of 20.2% left net margin at 26.5%, close to operating profitability [D215][D223].
Operating cash flow is not a meaningful earnings-quality measure for a bank; capital return is the better test [F60][F30].
Operating cash flow of $8.0 billion was 1.05x net income in FY2025, against a 1.24x FY2021 reading [F60][F30][D216][D114].
Buybacks plus dividends of $3.7 billion were 48.3% of FY2025 net income, up from $2.8 billion in FY2022 [D218][F30][D142].
Stock-based compensation was $235 million, 2.9% of operating cash flow [X37][D217].
Return on average equity was 12.2% in FY2025, above the 11.8% peer median and at the 71st percentile of seven banks [D226][D283][D282].
Loans were 73.5% of deposits, up from 67.2% in FY2021 as deposit growth outran lending [D224][D122].
The allowance was 2.0% of loans, and the credit-loss provision was 7.7% of revenue, at the 50th percentile of four peers against a 6.1% median [D225][D221][D284][D285].
Shareholders' equity rose 11.3% to $65.2 billion in FY2025 while the diluted share count fell 0.2% [D233][F114][D237].
Long-term debt is not reported after FY2022, so leverage after that year cannot be tracked from the filings [X172][R2].
Long-term debt stops being reported after FY2022 at $39.8 billion, a data break that blocks any post-2022 leverage comparison [X172][R2].
Revenue fell 2.4% in FY2024 as deposit repricing cut net interest income 6.4%, the one down year in the window [D214][D209][R1].
The provision stayed near 8% of revenue for four years, well above the 6.3% FY2016 level, so credit costs have not normalized [D221][D7].
If the efficiency ratio rises back above the 59.3% window median, the FY2025 cost improvement has reversed; it will show in the FY2026 10-K [D277][D220].
A net interest income decline below the FY2025 $16.6 billion level would signal deposit repricing is again outrunning asset yields [F10][P15].
Watch whether the provision falls below the 7.7% of revenue FY2025 level, which would confirm the improved credit quality cited for the latest decline [D221][P12].
